## Methods

Separation and screening of MAC and detrital fractions
For ODP Site 959 materials, authigenic clay residing in the >100 µm fraction were separated from the bulk sediment by wet sieving each sample, followed by treatment with 1M HCl to remove carbonates, phosphates and sorbed components18,61. Authigenic clay separates were subsequently triple rinsed with MilliQ water, oven dried and passed through a Frantz magnetic separator (0.6 and 0.2 A) to remove non-target phases such as biogenic opal, quartz, feldspar, organic matter and pyrite. Previous X-ray diffraction and microscopic characterization has demonstrated the high purity of MAC separates obtained in this manner from this site21,39, which we independently confirmed via optical and scanning electron microscope screening of our separates (Fig. 2).

We complement the Site 959 material with MACs separated from three near-surface intervals (8.6 to 11.1 cm depth) at an Oregon margin site (North Pacific, see Fig. 1) previously documented to contain sand-sized glauconitic smectite pellets10,25. Oregon Margin MACs were separated using the same approach outlined above, but were further split into a large (>250 µm) fraction, a less magnetic (0.6 to 0.4 A) 250–100 µm size fraction, and a more magnetic (0.4–0.2 A) 250–100 µm size fraction. Individual Oregon Margin MAC pellets are dominated by Fe smectite and glauconite10,25 but also contain modest amounts of detrital clay (chlorite, muscovite, and illite) and silicate (feldspar, quartz) inclusions (Fig. 2)10,25.

Assessment of elemental uptake or release during MAC formation requires comparison to the detrital precursor sediment from which MACs form. To this end, the host sediment of each MAC separate was also treated with 1M HCl before size separation into <5 µm and 5–100 µm (Site 959) or <5 µm, 5–20 and 20–100 µm (Oregon Margin) fractions using standard wet sieving and centrifugation approaches. We consider the <5 µm material to be a detrital clay fraction that does not contain MACs because previous work at these sites has shown that MAC formation is almost entirely restricted to sand size pellets10,20,25. This is confirmed by our scanning electron microscope (SEM) mineral mapping (Fig. 2) and quantitative X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses which do not identify Fe-smectite or glauconite in this fraction (see Supplementary Information). Similarly, the Oregon Margin 5-20 µm fraction does not contain MACs and can thus be considered detrital silt. The Oregon Margin 20–100 µm fraction, by contrast, contains abundant authigenic clay and is not appropriate for comparison (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Information). Based on this, and the relative abundance of detrital clay versus detrital silt at each site, we consider the MAC precursor phase to be the <5 µm detrital clay fraction at ODP Site 959 and the 5-20 µm detrital silt fraction at the Oregon Margin site.

SEM and XRD analyses
Samples for SEM characterization were prepared as 25 mm diameter polished resin mounts from intact, freeze-dried sediment. This involves vacuum impregnation of the samples in epoxy resin, polishing using diamond paste, and carbon coating prior to SEM analysis. Backscattered electron (BSE) images and SEM- energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mineral maps were obtained at Macquarie University using a FEI Teneo field emission SEM equipped with dual Bruker XFlash 6/30 EDS detectors. BSE images of the entire sample mount were collected using Thermofisher Scientific Maps Mineralogy software (V3.3). Smaller regions of interest on each mount were subsequently selected for higher resolution BSE imaging (<100 nm pixel resolution) and EDS mineral mapping (EDS spectrum collected every 1.5 µm, 12 ms acquisition time, ~8500 counts on quartz), followed by mineral identification using the Thermofisher Scientific Nanomin software (V3.3), following the approach recommended in ref. 62.

Samples for X-ray diffraction analysis (<100 µm detrital fractions only) were side-loaded into sample holders before collection of powder XRD patterns spanning 3.5° to 85° 2θ using a Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer with Lynxeye detector and a Co radiation source running at 40 kV and 40 mA, at a step size of 0.02° and 1 s dwell time per step. For Site 959, only <5 µm fractions yielded sufficient material for analysis, whereas all three Oregon Margin <100 µm fractions yielded sufficient material (Supplementary Information and Supplementary Data 5). Mineral identification and Rietveld-based quantification of powder XRD patterns was done using the Panalytical Highscore Plus software and its implemented pdf-4 database. Uncertainty on mineral abundances is <3%21.

Elemental and Nd isotope analyses
An aliquot of each authigenic clay separate (20-40 mg) and detrital clay or silt fraction (100 mg) was acid digested on a hot plate, using a 1:2 solution of distilled concentrated HNO3 and HF followed by 6M HCl. The resulting solutions were split, with an aliquot set aside for further purification and neodymium isotope (εNd) analyses. For the non-authigenic clay samples a volume corresponding to target masses of 0.5 µg Nd was set aside for Nd isotope analyses (see below for details). However, the authigenic clay aliquots only contained <0.07 µg Nd, so that not all samples yielded results with acceptable analytical precision for Nd isotopes.

Selected major and trace elements (45 elements in total) were analyzed at dilutions of 1:1,000 (trace elements) and 1:1,000,000 (major elements) on an Agilent 8900x ICP-MS/MS at Adelaide Microscopy (Adelaide University) along with a series of multi-element calibration solutions. Instrument conditions were: RF power 1550 W, sample depth 10 mm, Ar carrier gas flow rate 0.95 L min−1 and Ar make up gas 0.1 L min−1, with a MicroMist nebulizer and a Scott Type spray chamber. 7Li, 9Be and 11B were measured in no gas mode. P, Fe and Cr were analyzed in reaction mode using N2O (20% flow, 0.21 ml min−1) and the MO+ reaction products measured (e.g., 56Fe measured as 56-72Fe at mass 72). For the remaining elements the collision cell was run in He mode (4 mL min−1 He gas flow). The sample introduction system was rinsed in two stages with 5% and 2% HNO3 between each analysis. On-line addition of indium was used for internal standardization, with secondary drift correction to regularly interspersed standard solutions. Analysis of several replicates of the USGS certified reference materials BCR-2 and BHVO-2 shows that most elements returned concentrations within <10% of certified values, whereas B, Mg and Tl fell within 15%.

Isotope aliquots were purified using Polyprep columns filled with ~2 mL of AG Wx8 200-400 mesh and secondary columns filled with 1 mL Eichrom LN 50–100 resin to isolate the Nd fraction (see also ref. 63). Purified Nd fractions were loaded on Re filaments using 1 µL of activator (1N HCl: 0.3M H3PO4) and analyzed for 143Nd/144Nd using an ISOTOPX Phoenix TIMS equipped with an ATONA signal amplification system (Adelaide University). Instrumental fractionation was corrected to a conventional 146Nd/144Nd ratio of 0.7219, using an exponential mass fractionation correction for the internal normalization of the Nd isotope data or 143Nd/144Nd ratios. JNdi-1a and BCR-2 were run as reference materials for 143Nd/144Nd (average for BCR-2=0.512651) to monitor data quality.

Zr normalization and elemental enrichment factors
Clay authigenesis is associated with substantial uptake of porewater-sourced major cations, primarily Fe3+/2+, K+ and Mg2+ ions17, with major element data showing that up to ~40% of Congo Shelf MAC mass is externally sourced18. Normalization to an immobile element such as Zr, Hf, Ti, Nb or Al is required to correct for this dilution effect and obtain accurate elemental enrichment or depletion trends relative to the precursor sediment64. We choose to present major and trace element concentrations normalized to Zr (Supplementary Data 4), following a systematic assessment of potential immobile elements using the isocon diagram approach65. Zirconium is commonly utilized to correct for volumetric changes or enrichment/dilution effects during weathering64, under the assumption that Zr is mainly hosted in zircon grains that are resistant to physical and chemical breakdown. Several lines of evidence suggest that fine silt to clay-grade zircons are the primary Zr hosts in both precursor sediment and MAC separates. Isotopic surveys of river sediments have shown that zircon is the primary host of Zr and Hf even in mud grade sediments66, though this may not be the case for river clays67. While their small size and relatively low abundance usually makes them challenging to image, our SEM-EDS mineral mapping approach demonstrates that <5 µm-scale zircon grains commonly occur both in authigenic clay pellets and in the host sediment at all sites (Fig. 2). Further, we observe a strong positive linear correlation between Zr and Hf in our MAC dataset with a slope that is indistinguishable from that of the corresponding detrital <5 µm fraction; both have Zr/Hf ratios that are very similar to the modal Zr/Hf ratio of granitic zircons68 and the upper continental crust69. We therefore conclude that Zr and Hf are primarily hosted by zircon and behave as quasi-immobile elements that are not substantially impacted by clay transformation reactions. Consequently66, normalization of the elemental data to Hf results in trends indistinguishable from Zr normalization (see Fig. 3). Ti, Nb, Th and Al, on the other hand, show evidence of mobility during clay authigenesis and are not suitable for normalization in this particular study.

We calculated the enrichment factor (EF) for each element as the ratio of the Zr-normalized concentration in the MAC to the Zr-normalized concentration in the precursor sediment (i.e., detrital clay or silt size fraction) and categorize each element as enriched (EF > 1), depleted (EF < 1), or unchanged (EF ~ 1).

Calculation of global MAC-related elemental fluxes
Assuming that our Fe-smectite to glauconite MACs are a reasonable proxy for MACs as a whole (see caveats in main text), we utilize the average green MAC composition (Supplementary Data 3) and the corresponding elemental enrichment factor (Supplementary Data 4) to calculate the corrected mass fraction of each element that is released or consumed during MAC formation, allowing us to obtain a first-order estimate of the global MAC-related flux for each element:

GlobalFlux i = (( (Conc i / EF i ) * (EF i - 1) ) / MAC av_Si ) * Global Si Flux (1)

where GlobalFlux i is the global flux (in Tg/yr) out of the pore fluid and into MACs (positive flux values) or into the pore fluid (negative flux values) for element i, Conc i is the average concentration of element i in MACs (wt%), EF i is the Zr-normalized enrichment factor for element i, MAC av_Si is the average Si content of glauconitic smectite (combined average of 26.8 wt% Si for Oregon Margin and Site 959 MACS; 21, 25, 39) and Global Si Flux is the global annual Si uptake flux into MACs (132 ± 5.6 Tg/yr Si9;). We use a Monte Carlo simulation approach (100,000 simulations for each element) to account for the likely range in each variable, and report median, 10th and 90th percentile flux estimates (Table 1). For Monte Carlo simulations, Conc i is randomly drawn from a truncated normal distribution defined by the average and standard deviation for each element, with minimum concentration values ≥ 0. EF i is drawn from a uniform distribution spanning minimum and maximum enrichment factors for each element. High Ba concentration and Ba EF outliers in some Oregon Margin MAC separates (Supplementary Data 3) are excluded due to the presence of barite inclusions10, as are REE+Y for Congo Shelf samples. Values for Global Si Flux are drawn from a normal distribution defined by the size and uncertainty of the flux reported by Rahman et al.9.

My specific comments are provided below:
1. The use of Zr-normalization may be influenced by the source of detrital silicate materials in different regions, as Zr is generally derived from zircon that is enriched in felsic igneous rocks. I recommend the authors use more elements (e.g., Th, Sc etc.) to normalize the trace element contents. Another issue is if the authors have separated the MACs from the bulk sediments, what the phase of Zr or other trace elements typically in terrestrially detrital silicates in these MACs.
Normalisation to an ‘immobile’ element is essential to avoid dilution-induced systematic bias in our results (see also our first response to R3 for detailed explanation). Amongst the elements in our dataset, Al, Ti, Zr, Hf and Nb are most commonly considered or employed as ‘immobile’ elements for normalisation. It has been shown however that none of these elements is entirely immobile in the terrestrial or marine weathering environment (Kurtz et al., 2000), so that is a matter of identifying the least mobile element.
We have evaluated this using the isocon diagram approach (Grant, 1986; we show a single example below), where we compare the composition of precursor vs MAC pairs for each interval at each site. Immobile elements are expected to form arrays that define a line of constant slope on the isocon diagram, with enriched elements falling above and depleted elements falling below this line. We complement this with SEM-EDS imaging and mineral mapping of the sediments, revealing the identity and distribution of potential host phases of candidate immobile elements.
Our evaluation shows that Hf and Zr consistently falls on a common line on the isocon diagram for each precursor-MAC pair. In contrast, Al, Nb and Ti, consistently fall below this line. For Site 959 samples, Nb and Ti also tend to define a common line, but with a significantly lower slope than the Hf-Zr pair. For Oregon Margin samples Ti and Al commonly define a line with slope < Zr-Hf pair, with Nb falling well below both Zr-Hf and Ti-Al lines.
We infer that Zr-Hf behave as quasi-immobile elements because they are primarily hosted in weathering-resistant µm-scale zircons that are retained as inclusions in MACs, consistent with SEM-based observations of micron-scale zircons in both host sediment and authigenic clay pellets (see our new Figure 2). This is supported by the strong positive linear correlation between Zr and Hf in our MAC dataset with a slope that is indistinguishable from that of the corresponding detrital < 5 µm fraction; both have Zr/Hf ratios that are very similar to the modal Zr/Hf ratio of granitic zircons (38.5; Wang et al., 2010) and the upper continental crust (McLennan, 2001) – see plot below. We therefore conclude that both Zr and Hf are the most immobile elements in our studied sedimentary systems, and that these elements are not substantially impacted by marine authigenic clay formation.
Ti and Nb, in contrast, are mobilised and partly lost during MAC formation because of the breakdown of Nb-bearing Ti-phases such as ilmenite, rutile or anatase, the main Ti carriers in the strongly weathered continental detritus accumulating at Site 959. This is consistent with widely documented Ti mobility during weathering, and SEM evidence that the abundance of Ti-bearing phases in the matrix is higher than in MAC pellets. At the Oregon Margin site, Ti (and presumably Nb) are largely hosted in igneous (detrital) aluminosilicates, so that Al and Ti define a line reflecting modest loss. Thus, most of the liberated Al and Ti is either incorporated into secondary clays or Ti oxide phases, whereas Nb is amongst the most depleted element at this site, suggesting that MACs systematically exclude this element (due to the its high hydration state (coordination number = 9), inducing inner- and outer-sphere complexation on mineral surfaces rather than structural incorporation into clay mineral lattice structures).

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this article, Stefan Löhr and his co-authors report on the distribution of major and trace elements in authigenic clay assemblages extracted from green glauconitic pellets from two marine settings (Oregon margin and Gulf of Guinea). Their aim was to assess whether marine authigenic clay formation acts as a source or a sink for trace elements in the ocean. Taken together with previously published data for the Congo shelf, they infer an average global composition for marine authigenic clays and provide estimates for corresponding elemental fluxes to (or from) seawater. Overall, this is a nice contribution, which reinforces previous suggestions that authigenic clay formation in the marine environment strongly influences oceanic geochemical cycles. The paper reads well and should probably yield a wide interest from the community. I have however one issue to raise regarding methodology and the (plausibly misleading) use of Zr-normalization to assess elemental behaviour during green clay formation.
Specifically, I am not convinced by the need to normalize data to Zr before interpreting elemental patterns in authigenic clay separates. The Zr-normalization method is generally used in soil investigations to account for volumetric changes and bulk density loss that typically occur during chemical weathering of the unaltered rock (protolith) and its transformation into soil constituents. The context is quite different here as glauconite probably displays a bulk density similar to nearby detrital clays.
While we appreciate R3’s constructive review, we disagree on this important point. We consider immobile element normalisation essential for identifying elemental enrichment or depletion in MACs relative to their detrital clay precursors. Mass transfer of various elements produces a daughter material that is compositionally substantially distinct to its parent material. In our specific case, the Fe-smectite to glauconite series of clays contain very high Fe, K and Mg (sum concentration, on oxide basis, ranges between 25 and 45 wt%) relative to their detrital mineral precursors (sum to only 8.6 to 14.7 wt%) as illustrated in the summary table below (data is taken from Supplementary Data Files included in this submission).
In the case of the Congo MACs, for example, this means that ~40% of the final glauconite mass can be attributed to incorporation of externally sourced elements during MAC formation. And that is without even taking into account potential losses of Al and gains/losses of Si during MAC formation. Indeed, this substantial mass gain, accompanied also by increase in minerally-bound water in MACs, produces the volumetric increase which results in the characteristic expansion/growth cracks and cauliflower-like, lobate morphology of mature glauconite grains (e.g. Odin & Mather, 1981). This massive uptake of elements and water results in the dilution of other elements, without normalisation to an immobile element to correct for this process it will produce spurious depletions of elements that are in fact immobile during MAC formation. Moreover, unless corrected for, this effect will exaggerate the depletion of depleted elements and reduce the enrichment of enriched elements.
In short, while simply normalising to the precursor clay compositions as R3 suggests will correctly identify highly enriched and highly depleted elements, misleading results will be obtained for immobile elements or those only exhibiting subtle enrichments or depletions. Further, the obtained enrichment factors will be biased to lower values, which would affect our flux calculations. Consequently, we consider immobile element normalisation an important step for this study.
That being said, we are aware of the potential limitations of this approach, related in particular to the challenge of identifying a truly immobile element (e.g. Kurtz et al 2000). As outlined in our response to R2 above, we have carefully assessed all options and come to the conclusion that Zr or Hf are the most suitable elements for data normalisation.
Additionally, the assumption made by the authors that authigenic clays quantitatively incorporate Zr from precursor detrital clay assemblages is probably not correct, at least not for the case of the Congo shelf green pellets. At the Congo margin, authigenic clays display a Hf isotopic composition markedly different from the precursor kaolinite-rich material (Bayon et al., 2023). Because Hf and Zr are twin elements, this discrepancy points towards specific Zr mobility during green clay formation. Therefore, normalizing measured elemental abundances to Zr could potentially result in biased interpretation. For instance, in S. Löhr and co-authors’s study, it creates an apparent REE enrichment in glauconitic pellets from the Congo Shelf, which contradicts with the interpretation that can be drawn using shale-normalized REE patterns when compared to nearby detrital clays.
Based on our systematic assessment of potential immobile elements measured in Site 959 and Oregon Margin materials, we conclude that Zr and Hf are least mobile and thus best suited to an ‘immobile’ element correction (see response to R2).
We suggest that the potential discrepancy between Hf and Zr, and the Hf isotopic differences between Congo MACs and detrital clays raised by R3 are potentially related to an isotopically distinct phosphate-hosted Hf reservoir in Congo shelf materials which undergoes partial isotope exchange during MAC formation. In contrast, and by analogy to our observations on the Site 959 and Oregon Margin materials (see our new Figure 2), we would suggest that Zr is largely hosted in mostly inert µm-scale zircons in both detrital and MAC materials. Accordingly, we have chosen to normalise our results to Zr rather than Hf.
The apparent REE enrichment in Congo shelf MACs in our results is readily explained. Bayon et al (2023) report light REE bearing phosphates in Congo Shelf MACs, which would prevent light REE loss during MAC formation and, depending on the origin/timing of these phosphates, potentially even result in a net increase in LREEs via uptake from pore water. Consistent with this, we obtain Zr-normalised enrichment factors that average ~1.6 for the LREEs (see Supplementary Table 4), indicating LREEs are immobile or slightly enriched. HREEs, however, are hardly incorporated into these phosphates and so are consistently depleted, showing enrichment factors of ~0.7. This is very similar to Zr-normalised REE enrichment factors observed for the Oregon Margin MACs. The apparent discrepancy with the conclusions of Bayon et al 2023, who report that MACs are depleted in both LREE and HREEs (less for LREE, more for HREEs) is simply because those authors did not correct for dilution effects brought on by the massive uptake of Fe, K and Mg which we demonstrated above, in our response to R#3’s previous point.
A final minor comment regarding another imprecise statement about the use of Zr in this study : in line 500 (Methods), the authors argue that « Geochemical and isotopic surveys of river sediments have shown that the weathering resistant mineral zircon is the primary host of Zr and Hf even in fine-grained sediments ». Note that this is only correct in silt-size fractions, but not in river clays, in which the behaviour of both Hf and Zr is completely decoupled from the presence of zircons (see Bayon et al., 2016).
We have revised the text to acknowledge this. Nevertheless, our systematic SEM-EDS mineral mapping (see Figure 2) has revealed an abundance of clay-grade zircons in all samples, including not just in the mud matrix but also in the MAC pellets.
Consequently, in this study, I would recommend the authors to simply normalize measured elemental abundances to values for nearby detrital clays.
We have articulated why we do not consider this to be a suitable approach in our first response to R#3.
